status: unpublished editorial group; chapter completion gate pending
sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 25 in full, with Psalms 27,32,51,86,103,119, Isaiah 40 and James 1 before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Preserve the semicolon joining verses 1–2 and the heading Of David.

verses.title: To You I lift up my soul
verses.heading: The prayer begins by turning the whole self toward the LORD
verses.meaning: The opening addresses the LORD before naming the trouble. Lifting up the soul is a poetic way of entrusting one's life and deepest concerns to God, rather than describing a soul visibly rising from a body. The bundled heading names David, but does not identify a particular episode in his life. The semicolon matters: this first verse flows into the trust expressed in verse 2. Attention, dependence and vulnerability belong together in the opening movement. Prayer begins with a relationship, before it becomes a list of requests.
verses.contextTitle: The first line continues into trust
verses.context: Psalm 25:1–2 forms a connected opening address. Psalm 86:4 also speaks of lifting up the soul while asking for joy, showing how the same prayer image can hold need and trust together without specifying one historical scene.
explore: Lift up my soul
The image concerns the whole person turning toward God. An anonymous figure's open hands in the painting are an artistic response, not a posture required by the verse.
Of David
The source preserves this heading. It names a David connection without telling us which trouble, location or stage of life supplied the occasion.
verses.reflect: What part of your life would you like to bring honestly into prayer today? Is there something you find difficult to put into words?
verses.alt: An anonymous adult stands on an olive ridge with open hands beneath a wide dawn sky.

verses.title: Trust within vulnerability
verses.heading: Confidence in God is spoken alongside fear of disgrace
verses.meaning: The sentence from verse 1 continues with personal trust: my God. The speaker then asks not to be put to shame or become a cause for enemies to celebrate. Trust does not silence the threat or make the request unnecessary. The verse is a plea from someone exposed to opposition, not a report that the danger has already ended. Shame here involves the feared collapse of the speaker's hope before hostile observers; it does not prove that every feeling of embarrassment is a divine verdict. The enemies remain unnamed, so no modern person needs to be assigned that role.
verses.contextTitle: A petition follows the declaration of trust
verses.context: Verses 1–2 hold trust and a plea for protection in one sentence. Later in Psalm 25, the speaker names loneliness, distress and hostile hatred; the prayer remains candid about vulnerability while continuing to seek refuge.
explore: In You I trust
The speaker names the object of trust while still asking for help. This is dependence amid risk, rather than evidence that the situation already feels safe.
Do not let my enemies exult
The request asks that hostile opposition not triumph. It supplies neither an enemy's name nor permission to turn every disagreement into a sacred conflict.
verses.reflect: Where do trust and vulnerability sit beside one another in your life? What kind of support would help you face that situation honestly?
verses.alt: An anonymous traveler stands sheltered in a rocky cleft, looking toward an opening and distant path.

verses.title: Hope shared by those who wait
verses.heading: The personal plea widens into confidence for others
verses.meaning: The voice moves from my trust to all who wait for the LORD. Waiting is joined to hope, while the contrast exposes treachery rather than mere weakness or uncertainty. The singer expresses confidence that reliance on God will not finally be a disgrace. This line should not be used to deny the real humiliation faithful people can suffer, or to call someone treacherous because help has not arrived quickly. The rest of the psalm still asks for rescue. Its confident statement belongs within a prayer that continues to name fear, guilt and distress.
verses.contextTitle: A wider confidence within an unfinished prayer
verses.context: Verse 3 broadens the concern of verses 1–2, then verses 4–5 ask for teaching and guidance while waiting continues. Psalm 27:14 likewise encourages waiting, strength and courage without making waiting a sign of failure.
explore: None who wait for You
The speaker's hope includes a community beyond the individual. Waiting can include prayer, learning and responsible action rather than an instruction to do nothing.
Treachery without cause
The contrast names faithless wrongdoing. It is not a label to place on someone simply because they are distressed, confused or still seeking help.
verses.reflect: Who might be waiting through uncertainty alongside you? What could mutual encouragement look like without pretending either of you knows the outcome?
verses.alt: Three anonymous adults wait beside a stone roadside bench beneath a broad olive tree.

verses.title: Teach me Your paths
verses.heading: The prayer asks to learn the LORD's way of living
verses.meaning: The request turns toward guidance: show me and teach me. Ways and paths are images for a life shaped by the LORD, not only for choosing between travel routes or predicting the future. The following verses connect guidance with truth, goodness, humility and covenant faithfulness. Asking for direction therefore includes a willingness to learn and change. The verse does not describe a hidden sign or promise a private answer to every decision. It offers words for approaching uncertainty as a learner, with conduct as well as destination in view.
verses.contextTitle: Direction is connected to truth and character
verses.context: Psalm 25:4 introduces the guidance developed in verses 5 and 8–10. Psalm 86:11 similarly joins being taught God's way with walking in truth and an undivided heart; the path image concerns a way of life.
explore: Show me; teach me
Both requests leave room for learning. They do not claim that an existing preference must already be God's instruction.
Ways and paths
The parallel images look ahead to God's goodness, right judgment and loving faithfulness. A landscape path is symbolic art, not a map of a recorded journey.
verses.reflect: Where are you asking for direction? What might you need to learn, listen to or reconsider before deciding on your next step?
verses.alt: A winding stone footpath runs through sage grass and olive saplings, with a plain staff at its near edge.

verses.title: Guide me in Your truth
verses.heading: Learning and waiting rest in the God who saves
verses.meaning: The request for teaching continues, now naming truth and salvation. The speaker waits all day for the God who saves, holding need for rescue together with willingness to be taught. Waiting here is relational dependence, not a technique for forcing a result by a deadline. Truth gives direction to the learning; the aim is more than getting whatever outcome the speaker first wanted. The line allows a prayer for guidance to continue through ordinary hours. It does not require every uncertainty to disappear before a person can ask for help or take a careful step.
verses.contextTitle: Guidance continues through the day of waiting
verses.context: Verse 5 extends verse 4's request and repeats the waiting of verse 3. Isaiah 40:27–31 answers a weary community's fear of being overlooked with hope in the Creator's enduring strength; it is a related context, not the occasion of Psalm 25.
explore: In Your truth
Guidance is tied to what is true, rather than merely useful to the speaker. The next verses keep that teaching connected with mercy and moral goodness.
All day long
The prayer gives waiting a daily texture. It names sustained dependence without providing a schedule for rescue or a measure of someone's faith.
verses.reflect: What helps you stay open to learning while an answer takes time? Is there one honest and manageable step you can take today?
verses.alt: An anonymous traveler sits beside an unmarked stone milestone as a valley path stretches ahead in late afternoon light.

verses.title: Remember Your compassion
verses.heading: The appeal rests on God's enduring loving devotion
verses.meaning: The speaker asks the LORD to remember compassion and loving devotion. In prayer, this is an appeal for God to act according to His enduring character, not a claim that He has suffered a lapse of memory. The reason given reaches beyond the current crisis: these mercies are from age to age. Verse 7 will contrast remembering mercy with not remembering past sins. Together the lines ask that God's goodness, rather than the speaker's failures, shape the response. The appeal does not hide responsibility; it locates hope in compassion that precedes the present need.
verses.contextTitle: Remembering mercy before naming old sins
verses.context: Verses 6–7 form a connected appeal about remembrance, mercy and past wrongdoing. Psalm 103:8–14 also joins compassion, loving devotion and God's knowledge of human frailty, offering a companion passage for this prayer.
explore: Remember
The speaker asks for a response consistent with the LORD's character. The language belongs to relationship and petition, not an explanation of divine memory.
From age to age
The appeal rests on enduring compassion rather than a newly earned favor. The psalm will still ask for forgiveness and instruction in a changed way of life.
verses.reflect: What helps you remember compassion when the present feels overwhelming? Is there a kindness you want to bring back into view today?
verses.alt: An old olive tree with weathered roots and healthy leaves grows among hillside wildflowers.

verses.title: Remember me according to Your love
verses.heading: The speaker names past wrongdoing and appeals to goodness
verses.meaning: The prayer now names sins of youth and rebellious acts. Instead of denying them, the speaker asks not to be remembered by those failures, but according to the LORD's loving devotion and goodness. The contrast is between different grounds for God's response, not between honesty and forgetting responsibility. Nothing in the heading tells us which acts are in view, so David's later stories must not be inserted as this verse's hidden setting. The request offers words for repentance that looks beyond self-condemnation toward mercy, without requiring harmed people to dismiss what happened.
verses.contextTitle: Honest confession within an appeal for mercy
verses.context: Verse 7 follows the plea to remember enduring compassion and precedes the declaration that the LORD teaches sinners. Psalm 32:5 likewise joins acknowledging wrongdoing with forgiveness; it need not identify the same incident or speaker's circumstances.
explore: Sins of my youth
The speaker admits a history of wrongdoing but supplies no list. The line should not be turned into an invented story about a particular youthful act.
According to Your loving devotion
The appeal asks that mercy and goodness shape how the person is received. It does not claim that confession cancels the need for truth, repair or accountability.
verses.reflect: Is there something from your past you want to face with honesty and compassion? What might a responsible step toward repair or support look like?
verses.alt: A chipped earthen jar holds a fresh olive shoot beside worn linen on a quiet stone ledge.

verses.title: Goodness that teaches sinners
verses.heading: The declaration of God's character opens a way to learn
verses.meaning: After asking for mercy, the speaker declares that the LORD is good and upright. The therefore links that character with teaching sinners the way. God does not need to approve wrongdoing in order to instruct people who have done wrong. Goodness and uprightness belong together: mercy opens toward a changed way of living rather than leaving the person without direction. The next verse describes humility as the posture of learners. The statement offers hope for correction without making a person's worst act the whole of their identity or excusing its consequences.
verses.contextTitle: From a plea for mercy to a description of the teacher
verses.context: Verse 8 begins a reflection on guidance in verses 8–10, after the petitions of verses 4–7. Psalm 119:68 also joins God's goodness with a request to be taught, connecting praise and the desire to learn obedience.
explore: Good and upright
The paired descriptions hold kindness and moral faithfulness together. The verse does not make goodness depend on overlooking harm.
He shows sinners the way
Instruction is available to people who need correction. The following focus on humility discourages a posture of superiority toward other learners.
verses.reflect: Where would you welcome patient correction or a fresh start? What would help you learn without either excusing harm or treating yourself as beyond hope?
verses.alt: A gentle path leads from rough stones into an olive grove where two anonymous adults walk together.
